opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest test is whether the framework gets out of the model's way. A lot of agent frameworks were designed when models were weaker, so people built elaborate scaffolding: fixed workflows, many hand-written prompts, rigid planning steps, routing logic. That made sense when the model couldn't plan reliably. But as models get stronger, much of that scaffolding becomes a ceiling instead of a support. So the first thing I look at is whether the framework still works, and works better, when you swap in a stronger model. If performance saturates or even drops, the framework is encoding human assumptions that the model has already surpassed.

The second thing is context management. An agent's real bottleneck is often less raw reasoning than what information is in the context window at each step: how tool results are fed back, how long histories are compressed, whether errors and failures are preserved so the model can learn from them within the episode. A good framework treats context as a scarce resource and manages it carefully. A bad one either floods the model with noise or throws away exactly the information the model needed.

Third, the tools and the action space. Are the tools general and composable, like a shell, a file system, a browser, a code interpreter? Or are they narrow, task-specific APIs that only work for the demo? General tools let the model's own capability show. Narrow tools make the system brittle the moment the task drifts a little.

Fourth, I care a lot about whether it's friendly to training, not just inference. In the end, the strongest agent capability comes from training the model inside the environment it will actually be used in. So a good framework should produce clean trajectories, give verifiable feedback signals, and be easy to run at scale in sandboxes for reinforcement learning. If a framework is great for a demo but impossible to roll out thousands of times in parallel with reliable rewards, it's not really a foundation you can build on.

And finally, there's the practical, almost boring criterion: on real long-horizon tasks, how often does it finish, how often does it get stuck, and when it fails, can you understand why? Benchmarks help, but I trust actual usage more. If people who use it every day keep coming back because it saves them real work, that's the best signal.

So, in short: minimal human prior, good context engineering, general tools, trainability, and real-world robustness. And the framework should get simpler, not more complicated, as models get better.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of the frameworks people argue about don't matter nearly as much as they think, and the way I judge one is by asking how much it gets out of the model's way.

Let me explain what I mean. When we started building agents, the instinct was to compensate for the model. The model couldn't plan well, so you wrote a planner. It couldn't remember, so you built a memory module. It got lost in long tasks, so you broke everything into a rigid state machine with hand-written transitions. That's where a lot of frameworks came from, and they were useful at the time. But every one of those pieces encodes an assumption about what the model can't do. And those assumptions go stale very fast. Six months later the base model can do the thing natively, and your framework is now actively fighting it, forcing it down a path that was designed for a weaker model.

So my first test is: how much of this framework is scaffolding for a model that no longer exists? If I swap in a model that's two generations newer, does the framework get better, or does it get in the way? A good framework should get better almost for free. If it doesn't, the abstraction is in the wrong place.

The second thing I look at is whether it treats the environment seriously. I think people underestimate this. An agent is really a model plus an environment plus a loop. The model is given. The loop is simple. The environment is where all the actual engineering is: how tools are described, what the agent can observe, how errors come back, whether the feedback is informative. A framework that spends most of its complexity on orchestration and very little on making the environment legible to the model has its priorities backwards. I'd much rather have a thin loop and really well-designed tools than a sophisticated multi-agent hierarchy with sloppy tool interfaces.

Third is observability, in a very practical sense. Can I see exactly what the model saw at every step? Can I replay a trajectory? When something goes wrong, can I tell whether it was the model's mistake, a bad tool result, or the framework truncating or rewriting context behind my back? A surprising number of frameworks do things to the context silently, and that makes them almost impossible to debug and, frankly, impossible to train against. If you're doing any RL on top of the agent, that part is non-negotiable. The framework has to be a faithful recorder.

And then there's a softer criterion, which is: does it let you do the dumb simple thing first? The best frameworks let you write a loop with one tool and a while statement and have that work. Then they let you grow from there. The worst ones require you to understand twelve concepts before you can run hello world, and most of those concepts exist to solve problems you don't have yet.

So if I compress it: good frameworks are thin, they put their effort into the environment and tools rather than into controlling the model, they're transparent about context, and they age well as models improve. I'd honestly be a little suspicious of any framework that's very impressive on a demo today, because impressive usually means it's doing a lot, and doing a lot is exactly what tends to go stale.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with whether it helps the agent complete real tasks reliably. A demo that succeeds once doesn’t tell you very much. Can it handle different inputs, recover when a tool fails, and recognize when it needs to ask the user for help?

Then I’d look at how easy it is to understand failures. Can you see what information the agent had, which tools it called, and where it went wrong? If you can’t diagnose a failure, it’s difficult to improve the system.

And finally, does the framework justify its complexity? I’d compare it with a simple implementation using the same model and tools. If the framework makes development easier and improves reliability without adding too much cost or latency, that’s valuable. The number of features matters less than whether those features help you build something that works.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d judge it by whether it helps you build an agent that reliably finishes real tasks. A compelling demo is a start, but what happens when a tool fails, the context gets long, or the agent takes a wrong turn?

I’d look at three things: how easily you can express the workflow you need, how clearly you can see and diagnose what the agent is doing, and how well it performs on representative tasks—including success rate, latency, and cost.

And I’d compare it with a simple baseline. If a straightforward model-and-tools loop works just as well and is easier to maintain, the framework hasn’t yet earned its complexity.
